newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Moslem leading Serb in presidential vote.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Moslem leading Serb in presidential vote.

text.p: Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic, a Moslem, was leading the top Serb candidate for the senior job in a new collective presidency after post-war elections, with final results due later on Tuesday.

But the vote, the first since the end of the 43-month war and designed to integrate the shattered country, appeared set to return Croat, Moslem and Serb hardliners to power -- with moderate challengers left far behind.

Izetbegovic had 185,368 votes compared with 121,391 for Momcilo Krajisnik, speaker of parliament in the current Serb entity of Bosnia, with 38 of 109 municipalities reporting, said the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe.

The leader of Bosnia's main Moslem nationalist SDA party also boasted an 81 percent to 15 percent lead over his opposition rival for the Moslem seat on the presidency, former prime minister Haris Silajdzic, a moderate.
The senior member of the presidency would function as Bosnia's chief representative in foreign relations but the tripartite body is to govern by consensus.
Krajisnik, a hard-line nationalist, was also far ahead of his Serb opposition rival for the presidency, with 78 percent of the vote compared to 19 percent for centrist Mladen Ivanic.
In the race for the Croat seat on the presidency, nationalist Kresimir Zubak staked out a wide margin, 86 percent over 13 percent for moderate competitor Ivo Komsic.
Although Izetbegovic appeared to own a significant lead, victory was by no means assured yet with only a third of the municipalities accounted for by early on Tuesday.

Many tens of thousands of Moslem refugees, natural SDA supporters, registered to vote in Serb territory in hopes of regaining their homes sooner. But only Serbs were permitted to be listed on the presidential ballot in Serb territory.
That factor, as well as the possibility that Silajdzic splits the Moslem vote, could make the Izetbegovic-Krajisnik race very close in the final counting, analysts said.
On the other hand, Krajisnik's support is weakest in northern Bosnia where 70 percent of Serbs live. Preliminary results from northern Bosnia gave him a less substantial lead.
Initial results from voting for a new inter-communal Bosnian parliament are also expected on Tuesday.

The United States said it would work with Bosnia's election victors over the next month or so to establish new joint governing bodies, reversing the wartime partition of the country, and then focus on whether NATO forces should remain.

"We need to see how that (state-building) process unfolds before we can make a decision on whether or not there will be an need for a security force to stay on beyond the mandate of IFOR," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
IFOR is the 53,000-strong NATO-led force that separated and demobilised Bosnia's factional armies early this year in the key pre-election step mandated by the 1995 Dayton peace treaty.
President Bill Clinton has said 15,300 U.S. troops who form the nucleus of IFOR will leave Bosnia from mid-December. But many U.S. officials have acknowledged a successor force will be needed.
A team of international observers found no major irregularities in the vote, its director said in a preliminary report on Monday.

Coordinator for International Monitoring Ed van Thijn gave a generally upbeat post-mortem, making it likely the OSCE would certify the election outcome despite fraud allegations by parties and voters.
